---
title: "Dimension Reduction"
---

Dimension reduction compresses high-dimensional predictor spaces while
preserving useful structure for prediction, visualization, or
interpretation.

## Learning Objectives

- Explain principal components as directions of maximal variance.
- Distinguish PCA, principal components regression, and partial least
  squares.
- Recognize when dimension reduction helps and when it hides signal.
- Use resampling to choose the number of components.

## Core Ideas

Principal components replace the original predictors with orthogonal
linear combinations. PCR then fits a supervised model using the first
few components rather than all original predictors.

Suppose the centered and scaled predictor matrix is $X$. Principal
component analysis finds loading vectors $v_1, v_2, \ldots$ so that the
first score vector

$$
z_1 = Xv_1
$$

has the largest possible variance subject to $\|v_1\| = 1$. The second
component maximizes variance subject to being orthogonal to the first,
and so on. The result is a new coordinate system ordered by the amount
of predictor variation each component explains.

Scaling matters. Without scaling, variables measured on larger numeric
scales can dominate the components even when they are not more
important for the modeling question.

## PCA for Exploration

PCA is often used before modeling to inspect structure in many
predictors at once.

```r
library(ISLR)

college <- ISLR::College
x <- model.matrix(Apps ~ ., college)[, -1]

pca <- prcomp(x, center = TRUE, scale. = TRUE)
summary(pca)
biplot(pca, scale = 0)
```

The proportion of variance explained tells how much predictor variation
is represented by each component. The loadings show which original
variables define each component.

## Principal Components Regression

PCR uses principal components as predictors in a regression model. It is
especially useful when predictors are numerous and correlated.

```r
library(pls)

set.seed(571)
pcr_fit <- pcr(
  Apps ~ .,
  data = college,
  scale = TRUE,
  validation = "CV"
)

validationplot(pcr_fit, val.type = "MSEP")
```

Cross-validation chooses how many components to keep. Keeping too few
components can miss signal; keeping too many can reintroduce noise.

## PCA, PCR, and PLS

PCA is unsupervised: it uses only the predictors. PCR is supervised only
after the PCA step: it regresses the outcome on selected components.
Partial least squares is supervised during component construction: it
chooses components that are related to both $X$ and $Y$.

| Method | Uses outcome when constructing components? | Common use |
|---|---:|---|
| PCA | No | Visualization and compression |
| PCR | No | Regression with many correlated predictors |
| PLS | Yes | Prediction when directions of high predictor variance may not align with the outcome |

## Correlated Predictors Example

Use a data set with correlated predictors. Visualize the first two
components, then compare ordinary least squares, ridge, PCR, and PLS.

## Component Selection Practice

Practice by fitting principal components regression on a data set with
many correlated predictors. Use cross-validation to choose the number
of components, compare PCR with ordinary least squares and penalized
regression, and interpret what the first two components represent.
